hero.headline: House panel advances $1.15 trillion defense bill with accountability measures for Hegseth
hero.body:
The House Armed Services Committee advanced a $1.15 trillion defense policy bill early Friday, setting the stage for what would be the largest defense authorization in U.S. history. The legislation includes pay raises for service members, support for U.S. allies, and acquisition reforms.

The bill also includes provisions requiring increased accountability from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, reflecting bipartisan frustration with his leadership. The accountability measures come as some lawmakers from both parties have expressed concerns about oversight and transparency at the Pentagon under Hegseth's tenure.

The National Defense Authorization Act represents a significant increase in military spending and sets policy priorities for the Department of Defense. In addition to personnel pay increases, the legislation supports ongoing commitments to U.S. allies and implements reforms aimed at streamlining how the Pentagon acquires equipment and weapons systems.

The committee's vote sends the bill to the full House for consideration. The NDAA has historically enjoyed strong bipartisan support and is one of the few major pieces of legislation that Congress passes annually. The inclusion of provisions targeting Hegseth suggests lawmakers are using the must-pass bill as leverage to demand greater oversight of Pentagon operations.

The $1.15 trillion price tag reflects the scale of U.S. defense commitments worldwide and represents a continuation of increased military spending in recent years. The legislation will need to be reconciled with a Senate version before it can reach President Trump's desk for signature.

cards.headline: Iran Strikes US Military Base in Kuwait, Killing Multiple People at Airport
cards.body:
The United States and Iran are locked in an increasingly dangerous confrontation over Tehran's nuclear program, with President Donald Trump threatening military action and ordering a massive deployment of naval forces to the Middle East.

Trump has given Iran a deadline of 10 to 15 days to reach a nuclear deal or face what he called "really bad things." When asked whether he was considering limited military strikes to pressure Iran into negotiations, Trump told reporters: "I guess I can say I am considering" it. US military planning has reportedly advanced to an early stage, with options under consideration including targeted strikes against individuals and even pursuing leadership change in Tehran.

The military movements include repositioning of aircraft carriers and other warships in the region. However, it remains unclear whether these deployments are intended as intimidation tactics to force Iranian concessions on nuclear issues or as preparation for actual military operations.

Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi responded by rejecting military solutions. "That has been tested last year. There were huge attacks on our facilities, they killed and assassinated our scientists, but they couldn't kill our nuclear programme," he said in an interview.

Despite the military threats, diplomatic channels remain open. Araghchi held indirect talks in Geneva this week with Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. He said the two sides had reached an understanding on "guiding principles" but cautioned that a deal was not imminent. Araghchi indicated a draft counterproposal could be ready "in the next two or three days," with additional talks possible within a week.

The current tensions stem from Trump's decision during his first presidency to withdraw from an internationally backed nuclear agreement that had restricted Iran's program. After Trump exited the deal, Iran accelerated its nuclear activities. Last year, Israel conducted a 12-day military campaign against Iranian nuclear facilities, which the United States joined, though the campaign's long-term impact on Iran's nuclear ambitions remains unclear.

During Geneva discussions, the US did not demand zero uranium enrichment from Iran, and Iran did not offer to suspend enrichment activities. Instead, Araghchi said negotiations now focus on ensuring "Iran's nuclear programme, including enrichment, is peaceful and would remain peaceful forever."

A White House official responded to Araghchi's comments by reiterating that "the president has been clear that Iran cannot have nuclear weapons or the capacity to build them, and that they cannot enrich uranium."

The United Nations has expressed concern about the heightened rhetoric and increased military activities in the region. Trump also referenced a crackdown on protests in Iran, claiming 32,000 people were killed, though this figure could not be verified through independent sources.

cards.headline: Putin Rejects Meeting with Zelensky to Discuss Ending Ukraine War
cards.teaser: The Russian president said there is no point in meeting his Ukrainian counterpart despite an open letter calling for face-to-face peace talks.
cards.body:
Russian President Vladimir Putin dismissed the possibility of meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to negotiate an end to the war. Speaking at the St. Petersburg economic forum, Putin described Zelensky's open letter proposing face-to-face talks as rude and said he saw "no point" in such a meeting.

Putin reaffirmed Russia's commitment to achieving its war objectives in Ukraine, including seizing all of the eastern Donbas region. His remarks signaled an intention to continue the military campaign rather than pursue immediate diplomatic solutions.

cards.headline: Federal judge strikes down Trump immigration freeze affecting 39 countries
cards.body:
A federal judge has ruled that the Trump administration unlawfully barred applicants from 39 travel-ban countries from receiving decisions on asylum claims, work permits, green cards and citizenship applications.

The ruling represents a significant legal setback for the administration's immigration policies. The judge determined that the freeze on processing applications from these nations exceeded the government's authority and violated applicants' rights to have their cases reviewed.

The decision came on the same day the US Senate voted to pass legislation funding Trump's immigration enforcement agencies. The $70 billion bill passed 52-47 with no Democratic support after a marathon voting session that knocked down numerous proposed amendments. The funding supports US Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security for three years, ending a partial government shutdown that had lasted since February.

The immigration freeze had prevented tens of thousands of applicants from advancing their cases through normal channels. The Trump administration had defended the restrictions as necessary for national security purposes. However, critics argued the policy lacked clear justification and created humanitarian hardships for people seeking legal entry to or residence in the United States.

The ruling requires the government to resume processing applications from the 39 designated countries under standard procedures. The decision does not automatically grant immigration benefits to affected applicants but allows their cases to proceed through normal review processes. The practical impact will unfold as immigration agencies work through the backlog of cases that accumulated during the freeze period.

Separately, a federal judge in New York issued an order restricting immigration enforcement actions in federal courthouses. US District Judge P. Kevin Castel ruled that ICE agents cannot arrest immigrants in or around three federal courthouses in lower Manhattan except under exceptional circumstances. The ruling came in response to a lawsuit brought by civil liberties organizations including the ACLU and Make the Road NY.

Castel noted that while there is "a strong governmental interest in enforcing immigration laws," there is also a serious interest in allowing individuals to attend removal proceedings and pursue asylum claims "without fear of arrest." The order applies to immigration courts at 26 Federal Plaza and two other Manhattan locations. Castel indicated that a court case before him would likely result in a ruling that it was "arbitrary and capricious" for the Trump administration to withdraw 2021 policies regarding enforcement actions inside courthouses.

The Justice Department has not announced whether it will appeal the ruling on the 39 countries. Immigration advocates have welcomed the decision as a restoration of legal processes for thousands of people whose cases had been frozen.

cards.headline: Texas works to contain first screwworm case in US since 1960s
cards.teaser: Health officials are responding to the first case of screwworm in the United States since the 1960s, detected in Texas.
cards.body:
Texas authorities are responding to the first New World screwworm detected in the United States since 1966. The parasitic insect, which feeds on flesh, poses a threat to livestock and other animals in the southern region. Officials have confirmed there are no food safety concerns related to the discovery.

To combat the outbreak, the US is deploying sterile flies and dogs as control measures. Governor Greg Abbott has criticized the current production of sterile flies as inadequate for containing the parasite's spread. Ranchers in the affected areas are concerned about the potential reemergence of a pest that had been eradicated from the country for decades.

cards.headline: Stock Markets Fall Sharply as Strong Jobs Report Dims Rate Cut Hopes
cards.body:
U.S. stock markets experienced a significant selloff on Friday, with major indices closing sharply lower after a strong employment report sparked concerns about interest rate policy. The S&P 500 fell 2.6 percent in its worst single-day decline of the year, while the Nasdaq dropped 4 percent in its steepest fall since April 2025. The Dow declined 695 points. The losses ended nine consecutive weeks of market gains.

The market downturn was driven by disappointing expectations about Federal Reserve rate cuts. Employers added 172,000 jobs in May while the unemployment rate remained at 4.3 percent, demonstrating continued resilience in the labor market despite economic headwinds. This robust hiring data convinced investors that the Fed would maintain elevated interest rates for longer than previously anticipated, triggering a sharp rise in Treasury yields with the 10-year yield climbing above 4.53 percent.

Higher interest rates for an extended period could slow economic growth and reduce corporate profitability, especially for growth-focused companies that depend on lower rates to justify their valuations. Technology stocks bore the heaviest losses, with semiconductor companies hit particularly hard. Chipmakers and other AI-related stocks tumbled across the board, with shares in companies like Nvidia and other data analytics firms experiencing significant declines despite some reporting improved revenue outlasts.

The market weakness extended beyond the United States. Asian markets followed with their sharpest slides in seven months, as indices in Japan and South Korea dropped more than 5 percent from recent record highs. European markets in the UK, France and Germany also declined slightly.

Several major bank executives warned of potential market corrections ahead. The chief executives of Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs joined JPMorgan Chase's Jamie Dimon in cautioning about market vulnerability. Analysts noted growing concerns about technology company valuations, particularly in the artificial intelligence sector. Many investors have highlighted that the vast majority of AI investment has been concentrated in a small group of companies, yet meaningful returns on these investments remain elusive.

The strong jobs report revealed underlying economic tensions. While headline employment figures appeared robust, wage growth has not kept pace with inflation, and consumer sentiment remains pessimistic. Young workers entering the job market face particular challenges starting their careers, a situation researchers indicate can have lasting effects on lifetime earnings and career advancement.

The market volatility also extended to riskier assets. Bitcoin briefly dipped below $100,000 for the first time since June as investors withdrew money from speculative investments amid broader economic concerns. The cryptocurrency had reached record highs above $126,000 in early October but has since faced significant downward pressure.

cards.headline: Treasury Yields Jump Above 4.5 Percent After Jobs Data
cards.teaser: The 10-year Treasury yield surged above 4.53 percent as strong employment numbers reduced expectations for rate cuts.
cards.body:
Treasury yields rose sharply Friday following stronger-than-expected employment data. The 10-year Treasury yield climbed above 4.53 percent as investors reassessed expectations for Federal Reserve rate cuts, with bond traders now pricing in reduced odds of cuts this year.

The market turmoil extended to equities, where the S&P 500 fell more than 2.6 percent—its worst single day of the year and ending nine weeks of consecutive gains. The Dow dropped 695 points while the Nasdaq fell 4 percent, with significant losses concentrated in the technology sector.

cards.headline: France Opens Investigation Into Israeli Treatment of Gaza Flotilla Activists
cards.teaser: Activists detained while attempting to reach Gaza said they were abused in Israeli custody, prompting French authorities to launch a formal probe.
cards.body:
France has launched an investigation into allegations that Israeli authorities mistreated pro-Palestinian activists detained during a flotilla operation aimed at reaching the Gaza Strip. The activists reported abusive treatment while in Israeli custody.

Israeli authorities have denied the mistreatment claims. The flotilla was intercepted before reaching Gaza, and its participants were taken into custody by Israeli forces.

cards.headline: European Union Leaders Say Montenegro Could Join Bloc by 2028
cards.teaser: European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the Balkan nation is within reach of membership after a regional summit.
cards.body:
European Union leaders gathered at a summit in Montenegro to discuss the bloc's expansion into the western Balkans. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Montenegro could be within reach of joining by 2028. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz emphasized that the EU must demonstrate both its capability and willingness to accept new members.

Leaders acknowledged the need to make the enlargement process faster and more credible. The summit brought together EU officials with representatives from six western Balkan countries seeking membership, reflecting the bloc's focus on integrating nations in southeastern Europe.

cards.headline: Nearly 50 People Die of Thirst After Lorry Breaks Down in Sahara Desert
cards.teaser: Only two survivors trekked more than 50 kilometers across the desert to alert authorities after the vehicle malfunctioned.
cards.body:
Nearly 50 people died of thirst in the Sahara desert after their lorry broke down. Only two survivors managed to trek more than 50 kilometers across the desert to reach authorities and alert them to the stranded group's plight.

By the time rescue efforts could be organized, the remaining passengers had succumbed to dehydration in the extreme desert conditions.

cards.headline: Everest Guide Survives Six Days on Mountain After Separation from Group
cards.teaser: Dawa Sherpa, 57, was found alive after eating chocolate and chewing ice during a prolonged ordeal on the world's tallest mountain.
cards.body:
A 57-year-old Sherpa guide survived six days alone on Mount Everest after becoming separated from his group. Dawa Sherpa was found alive by a cleaning crew as he descended the mountain and later spoke to the BBC from a hospital about his ordeal.

During his time on the mountain, Sherpa sustained himself by eating chocolate and chewing ice. His wife has questioned whether more could have been done to locate him sooner, raising concerns about search and rescue procedures on Everest.

cards.headline: Astronauts Return to Space Station After Sheltering During Air Leak Repair
cards.teaser: Five astronauts took shelter as Russian crew members attempted to repair a leak in a tunnel area of the International Space Station.
cards.body:
Astronauts aboard the International Space Station have resumed normal duties after being placed on evacuation alert due to an air leak. NASA ordered five crew members, including two US astronauts, a French astronaut, and a Russian cosmonaut from the Crew-12 mission, to enter their docked Crew Dragon spacecraft and don spacesuits as a precaution.

Russian specialists discovered two air leaks while pressurizing the transfer chamber of the Zveda module. After the repair work was paused, mission control cleared the crew to return to regular operations on Friday morning.

cards.headline: Murder trial begins for fatal stabbing at Texas high school track meet
cards.teaser: The trial of Karmelo Anthony opened with prosecutors arguing the stabbing death of Austin Metcalf was murder, not self-defense.
cards.body:
Jurors in Frisco watched videos of the stabbing during opening statements in the murder trial of Karmelo Anthony, who is accused of killing Austin Metcalf at a Frisco ISD track meet. Prosecutors told the jury the fatal stabbing was murder and rejected defense claims of self-defense.

The trial has drawn attention partly because no Black jurors were seated on the panel in a case involving a racially charged incident. Testimony is ongoing, with witnesses providing accounts of what happened at the track meet where the stabbing occurred.

cards.headline: Trump says he wants acting intelligence director to cut the office
cards.teaser: President Trump said he instructed his acting director of national intelligence to reduce the size of the office.
cards.body:
President Trump has urged Bill Pulte, his acting director of national intelligence, to fire "a lot of people" from the intelligence agencies. Trump noted that Pulte, who has no previous experience in intelligence, is "less shackled" because he holds only a temporary appointment rather than a formal nomination.

Trump stated he wants to see the intelligence agencies shrink, claiming current staffing levels are "way too high." The appointment has proven controversial, with the Senate blocking a surveillance program extension amid concerns over Pulte's nomination.

cards.headline: British actor Anthony Head dies at 72
cards.teaser: Anthony Head, known for roles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Ted Lasso, died from complications of pneumonia.
cards.body:
British actor Anthony Head has died at age 72 from complications related to pneumonia. The actor appeared in numerous television series including Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Ted Lasso, Merlin, and Little Britain throughout his career.

Head first gained public recognition in the 1980s through his appearances in Nescafe coffee advertisements before moving into dramatic television roles. His daughter India announced his death on Instagram.

cards.headline: Mother of missing Auburn student in Japan says they argued before disappearance
cards.teaser: The mother of an Auburn University student missing in Japan said they had an argument about ChatGPT before he vanished.
cards.body:
The mother of an Auburn University student who disappeared in Japan said she and her son argued about ChatGPT before he went missing. She expressed fear that he may have gotten hurt or become stuck after vanishing in a mountainous forest area.

Japanese citizens are joining the search for the missing American in the difficult terrain. The Alabama community is praying for the student as the search continues, and the family has made a new public request for assistance in locating him.

cards.headline: Maine Senate candidate denies accusations of rough treatment of former girlfriends
cards.teaser: Graham Platner denied New York Times allegations of being physically rough with ex-girlfriends, calling controversies a sign of momentum.
cards.body:
Graham Platner is staying in the Maine Senate race despite a New York Times report detailing accusations that he was physically rough with former girlfriends. Platner has rejected the allegations outright.

The candidate views the recent controversies, including the Times report, as signs that his campaign is gaining traction rather than cause for concern. He characterized the accusations as attacks designed to undermine his Senate bid and has vowed to continue his campaign.

cards.headline: Google to Pay SpaceX $920 Million Monthly for Computing Capacity
cards.teaser: Google agreed to pay SpaceX nearly $1 billion per month for compute capacity at data centers.
cards.body:
Google will pay SpaceX $920 million each month for computing capacity, according to reports Friday. The deal represents one of the largest cloud computing agreements disclosed to date and reflects the massive infrastructure investments required for artificial intelligence development.

The computing capacity will be provided at xAI data centers. The arrangement underscores the growing competition among technology companies to secure the processing power needed for training and running advanced AI models. The monthly payment total approaches $11 billion annually.

cards.headline: Bitcoin Drops Below $60,000 for First Time Since 2024 Election
cards.teaser: Bitcoin fell below $60,000, reaching its lowest level since October 2024.
cards.body:
Bitcoin fell below $60,000 on Friday, reaching its lowest level since President Trump's election victory in 2024. The decline reflects a broader shift in investor interest away from cryptocurrencies toward other asset classes.

Companies with significant bitcoin holdings, including Strategy Shares, have seen their stock prices decline as a result. Investors have increasingly moved capital into artificial intelligence stocks and major initial public offerings, signaling a change in market preference away from digital assets.

cards.headline: Trump to Meet AI Company Leaders Next Week on Investment Plans
cards.teaser: President Trump said he expects to meet with leaders of top AI companies to discuss possible government investment.
cards.body:
President Trump said Friday he expects to meet with leaders of major artificial intelligence companies next week to discuss potential government investment in the sector. The administration is exploring ways to take equity stakes in AI firms as part of efforts to maintain American leadership in artificial intelligence development.

The meetings will center on government partnerships and profit-sharing arrangements with AI companies. These discussions reflect the administration's broader strategy to shape how the technology industry develops.

cards.headline: Small Nuclear Reactor Reaches Criticality in Idaho Test
cards.teaser: A small modular nuclear reactor reached criticality for the first time at Idaho National Laboratory.
cards.body:
The Mark-Zero advanced nuclear reactor reached criticality at Idaho National Laboratory, the Department of Energy announced Friday. The privately developed small modular reactor represents the first advanced reactor to reach this operational milestone in the United States.

Reaching criticality means the reactor achieved a sustained nuclear chain reaction, a key step in demonstrating the technology's viability. Small modular reactors are designed to be manufactured in factories and transported to sites, potentially reducing construction costs and timeframes compared to traditional nuclear plants. The technology is viewed as a potential source of carbon-free electricity.

cards.headline: Job Market Strength Leaves Recent Graduates Struggling
cards.teaser: People entering the workforce are having difficulty starting careers despite overall labor market improvement.
cards.body:
Young graduates are struggling to launch their careers even as the overall job market strengthens. While employers added 172,000 jobs in May and hiring has maintained a vigorous pace, entry-level opportunities remain scarce for new workers entering the workforce.

This mismatch between broad labor market health and limited early-career positions carries serious consequences. Research shows that difficult workforce entry can permanently impact lifetime earnings and career progression, with workers who start during weak hiring cycles earning significantly less than those who begin during stronger periods.

hero.headline: NASA orders astronauts to shelter in spacecraft during ISS air leak repair
hero.body:
NASA directed five astronauts aboard the International Space Station to shelter in their docked Dragon spacecraft and prepare for a possible evacuation while Russian space officials attempted to repair air leaks in the station's Russian segment.

The four crew members of NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 mission and a fifth American astronaut, Chris Williams, who had been aboard the station for 190 days, received the shelter-in-place order. The astronauts included American astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, French astronaut Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency, and Russian cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev. Two other Russian cosmonauts, Sergey Kud-Sverchkov and Sergey Mikayev, remained aboard the station.

The air leaks were discovered in the transfer tunnel of the Zvezda Service Module during pressurization of the module's transfer chamber. Roscosmos specialists identified two leak sites. They quickly sealed one leak using a two-component sealant called Germetal-1. The second potential leak was located on the conical portion of the transfer chamber. Russian officials stated there was no immediate threat to crew safety or station systems.

After approximately two hours of sheltering, NASA instructed the five astronauts to end safe-haven procedures and return to normal operations aboard the station. The decision came as Roscosmos paused structural repair efforts to assess additional measurements and data from the leak sites.

"Given this development, NASA has instructed the crew members inside the Dragon spacecraft to end the safe haven procedures and return to planned operations aboard the International Space Station. We look forward to working with Roscosmos on a collaborative approach to address the leaks," said Bethany Stevens, a NASA spokesperson.

The Zvezda Service Module, which measures approximately 43 feet long, serves as a critical component of the station. It contains living quarters, life support systems, communications equipment, electrical power distribution, data processing systems, flight control systems, and propulsion systems. The module was the first fully Russian contribution to the ISS and includes docking ports for Russian Soyuz and Progress spacecraft.

Air leaks have presented a persistent challenge for the Russian segment of the space station. Roscosmos has dealt with cracks and leaks in its station compartments for more than five years, with NASA's Office of Inspector General identifying them as a top safety risk. In June, a chartered spaceflight carrying astronauts from India, Poland, and Hungary was postponed due to similar leak concerns.

The International Space Station operates as a collaborative effort between NASA, the Canadian Space Agency, the European Space Agency, Japan's space agency, and Roscosmos. The station has maintained continuous human occupation for 25 years, orbiting approximately 250 miles above Earth.

cards.headline: Google to pay SpaceX $920 million per month for compute capacity
cards.teaser: The companies announced a major compute deal one week before SpaceX's planned initial public offering.
cards.body:
Google and SpaceX announced an agreement under which Google will pay SpaceX $920 million per month for compute services. The deal was revealed on a Friday, just days before SpaceX is scheduled to go public through an initial public offering.

The compute arrangement represents a significant commercial agreement between the two technology companies. SpaceX has been preparing for a historic IPO, and the Google deal adds a major revenue stream ahead of the public market debut.

cards.headline: S&P 500 declines to waive profitability rule for SpaceX ahead of IPO
cards.teaser: The index operator will not grant SpaceX early access despite the company's upcoming public offering.
cards.body:
The S&P 500 will not make an exception to its profitability requirements for SpaceX following its initial public offering. This means SpaceX cannot immediately join the index, limiting its access to the vast capital flows from passive investors tracking the benchmark.

The index typically requires companies to prove profitability before inclusion. SpaceX had sought a waiver to accelerate entry and tap into billions of dollars from index funds. The decision also sets a precedent for other unprofitable companies, including artificial intelligence firms, seeking similar treatment.

cards.headline: Former IBM cybersecurity executive accuses company of covering up data breaches
cards.teaser: A lawsuit alleges IBM and two subsidiaries were breached in the mid-2010s but did not disclose the incidents.
cards.body:
A former cybersecurity executive has filed a lawsuit accusing IBM and two subsidiary companies of failing to disclose data breaches that occurred during the mid-2010s. According to the lawsuit, IBM actively covered up these security incidents rather than reporting them to affected parties or regulators.

The case highlights IBM's handling of cybersecurity incidents during that period and raises questions about whether the company met its disclosure obligations to those impacted by the breaches.

cards.headline: Supabase valuation doubles to $10 billion in eight months
cards.teaser: The open source database platform has grown rapidly with help from AI coding tools.
cards.body:
Supabase has reached a $10 billion valuation, doubling its worth in just eight months. The company exemplifies how open source projects can evolve into thriving commercial ventures.

The company's growth has been fueled by AI-assisted coding tools like Claude and Codex, which have helped accelerate developer adoption of Supabase's database and backend services. These AI platforms have made it easier for developers to build new applications using Supabase's infrastructure.

cards.headline: Data center developer cuts project size 50% after community protests
cards.teaser: The company said it felt beaten up and had no choice but to shrink the planned facility.
cards.body:
A developer has reduced the size of a planned data center by half following sustained protests from local residents. The company acknowledged that the project generated significant opposition, saying it pissed off many people in the community.

The developer stated it felt beaten up by the backlash and believed it had no choice but to scale back the facility. The reduced project represents a compromise between the company's infrastructure needs and community concerns about the data center's impact on the area.

cards.headline: GM accelerates new battery technology deployment for cheaper electric vehicles
cards.teaser: The automaker wants to introduce cost-cutting battery tech up to a year earlier than planned.
cards.body:
General Motors is accelerating its deployment of new battery technology by up to a year to drive down electric vehicle prices and compete more effectively with gas-powered cars. A key manufacturing facility is central to this strategy, as it will scale up production of the advanced batteries needed across GM's EV lineup.

By bringing this battery technology to market faster than originally scheduled, GM aims to make electric vehicles more affordable and accessible to consumers while maintaining its competitive position in the rapidly evolving automotive market.

hero.headline: NCAA rules four former Alabama State players permanently ineligible for fixing game
hero.body:
The NCAA announced that four former Alabama State basketball players, including the standout performer from the team's historic first NCAA tournament victory, have been permanently banned from college sports. The players were ruled ineligible for accepting payments from gamblers to manipulate the outcome of a game during the 2024-25 season.

The permanent ineligibility marks one of the most severe penalties the NCAA can impose and represents a significant point-shaving scandal in recent college basketball. The four players allegedly accepted money from gamblers in exchange for intentionally influencing the final score of a game that season. An NCAA investigation uncovered evidence supporting the arrangement, leading to the permanent ban from college athletics.

The decision is particularly notable because one of the banned players was instrumental in Alabama State's breakthrough NCAA tournament win, a milestone moment for the Southwestern Athletic Conference program. The investigation's findings overshadowed what had been celebrated as a historic achievement for the university's basketball program.

Permanent ineligibility means the four players can never compete in NCAA-sanctioned athletics again. This represents the most severe penalty available to the NCAA for violations involving gambling and game manipulation. The investigation specifically examined the players' conduct during the 2024-25 season, when they were active roster members.

The NCAA announcement did not provide specific details about which game was allegedly fixed or the amount of money involved in the scheme. Point-shaving scandals, where players intentionally affect the margin of victory rather than the game's outcome, have surfaced periodically throughout college basketball history. However, cases resulting in permanent bans for multiple players from the same program remain relatively uncommon.

The ruling underscores growing concerns about gambling's influence on college sports. These concerns have intensified as legal sports betting has expanded significantly across the United States in recent years, creating new opportunities for potential manipulation and corruption. The NCAA has increasingly focused on protecting the integrity of collegiate athletics against gambling-related violations.

The case reflects broader challenges facing college sports as the landscape of legal gambling continues to evolve. Athletic programs and governing bodies must balance the expansion of legal betting with the need to protect players and maintain competitive integrity. The permanent bans signal the NCAA's commitment to enforcing strict penalties for gambling violations, particularly when multiple players from the same team are involved in coordinated schemes.

This scandal serves as a cautionary example of how gambling can compromise college basketball, even at programs experiencing their most successful moments. The investigation's findings demonstrate that success on the court does not shield programs from internal corruption and the temptations that can accompany expanded gambling opportunities in sports.

cards.headline: NASCAR Hall of Famer Ned Jarrett dies at 93
cards.teaser: The two-time Cup champion and longtime broadcaster died Thursday at his North Carolina home.
cards.body:
NASCAR Hall of Famer Ned Jarrett died peacefully Thursday from natural causes at his home in Newton, North Carolina. He was 93.

Jarrett was a two-time NASCAR Cup champion and had a distinguished career as a broadcaster for the sport following his racing days.

cards.headline: Bears move closer to relocation after board approves Indiana stadium plan
cards.teaser: The team's board of directors voted Thursday to advance development plans for a new stadium in Hammond, Indiana.
cards.body:
The Chicago Bears advanced their plan to relocate after the team's board of directors voted to move forward with stadium development in Hammond, Indiana. The decision marks a significant step in the franchise's efforts to leave Chicago.

Hammond is located in northwest Indiana near the Illinois border. The board's approval enables the team to continue with planning and negotiations for the stadium project.

cards.headline: NBA interviews Kawhi Leonard in Clippers salary cap probe
cards.teaser: League investigators questioned the star and his business adviser as part of an investigation into alleged cap circumvention.
cards.body:
NBA investigators have questioned LA Clippers star Kawhi Leonard and his business adviser as part of an ongoing investigation into whether the team circumvented salary cap rules to compensate Leonard outside official team channels.

The probe examines allegations that the Clippers provided compensation to Leonard through unofficial means, which would violate league salary cap regulations. Both Leonard and his adviser participated in interviews with NBA investigators.

cards.headline: Baker Mayfield says Buccaneers contract talks not close to expectations
cards.teaser: The quarterback said extension negotiations are far from what he anticipated and called for a long-term deal.
cards.body:
Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield publicly addressed contract extension negotiations for the first time this offseason, expressing dissatisfaction with discussions so far. He stated that talks are "not anywhere close to what we were thinking," signaling a significant gap between his expectations and the team's current offers.

Mayfield emphasized the need to reach a long-term agreement, calling for the Buccaneers to finalize a deal. His comments indicate ongoing tension in negotiations as both sides work toward resolving the quarterback's future with the franchise.

cards.headline: Aaron Judge says rib fracture originated from April diving catch
cards.teaser: The Yankees outfielder said the stress fracture stems from diving for a ball in late April.
cards.body:
New York Yankees outfielder Aaron Judge said the stress fracture in his right rib originated from diving for a ball in late April. The injury has kept Judge out of the lineup as he recovers from the fracture.

Judge identified the specific play that caused the initial damage, pointing to a diving defensive attempt during a game in the final week of April. The injury developed into a stress fracture that required time away from play.

cards.headline: US coach Pochettino frustrated as Chris Richards ruled out of World Cup tuneup
cards.teaser: The first-choice center back will miss the team's final friendly before the tournament with an ankle injury.
cards.body:
United States coach Mauricio Pochettino expressed frustration after revealing that center back Chris Richards would miss the team's final World Cup tune-up friendly against Germany due to an ankle injury. Pochettino said he was "not happy" with Crystal Palace's injury assessment of the defender.

Richards's status for the World Cup itself is now in doubt as Pochettino awaits further medical evaluations. The loss of his first-choice center back deprives the team of a crucial final preparation match before the tournament begins.

hero.headline: Anthony Head, Star of Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Ted Lasso, Dies at 72
hero.body:
British actor Anthony Head has died at age 72 from complications of pneumonia. His daughters Emily and Daisy confirmed the news, stating he "passed away peacefully of complications due to pneumonia, surrounded by his family."

Head became an international fixture on television through his role as Rupert Giles in Buffy the Vampire Slayer. He played the school librarian and mentor to Sarah Michelle Gellar's character throughout the show's seven-season run from 1997 to 2003. His portrayal of the tweedy father figure made him one of the series' most recognizable cast members.

Before Buffy brought him global recognition, Head had built a substantial career in British entertainment. He began on stage, appearing in the 1978 West End revival of Godspell alongside Su Pollard and later playing Freddie Trumper in the original West End production of the Abba musical Chess in 1988. He also performed in the 1990 West End production of The Rocky Horror Show as Dr. Frank-N-Furter.

Head gained significant public attention in Britain during the 1980s for his role in Nescafe Gold Blend television commercials, which featured a slow-burn courtship between two neighbors. Beyond those ads, his film work included roles in the 1981 adaptation of Lady Chatterley's Lover and 1987's A Prayer for the Dying alongside Bob Hoskins and Liam Neeson. He also sang backing vocals for the British pop group Red Box, appearing on their 1986 debut album.

After securing the Buffy role, Head relocated to Los Angeles for five years while his partner Sarah and two daughters remained in England. He made frequent trips home, traveling every three to four weeks whenever the production schedule allowed.

Following Buffy's conclusion, Head continued working across various projects. He took a recurring role in the BBC sketch show Little Britain, playing a British prime minister fawned over by a flirtatious assistant played by David Walliams. He appeared in the BBC production of Merlin and the film The Inbetweeners Movie. More recently, he played Rupert Mannion, a former football club owner, in the Emmy-winning Apple TV Plus series Ted Lasso, which concluded in 2023.

His Buffy co-stars have paid tribute to his memory. Sarah Michelle Gellar began her Instagram tribute with a Buffy quote: "Tell Giles I figured it out and I'm ok." She then wrote, "Well I don't have it figured out and I'm not ok. But I know I'm the lucky one because I knew you."

Head's daughters honored their father's legacy, noting that "he loved his job very much and he always considered himself incredibly lucky to have been able to work alongside such exceptionally talented people, in such wonderful productions, across a career that spanned several decades."

cards.headline: Actor James Handy Stabbed to Death in Los Angeles, Girlfriend's Son Arrested
cards.teaser: James Handy, who appeared in Top Gun: Maverick, was found stabbed to death in Tarzana, with the suspect allegedly flagging down police.
cards.body:
James Handy, an actor known for his role in Top Gun: Maverick, was found fatally stabbed in Tarzana, California. The girlfriend's son was arrested in connection with the killing. According to reports, the suspect allegedly flagged down police to tell them he was the person they were looking for.

Handy had a long career as a character actor in film and television. His most recent notable role was in the 2022 blockbuster Top Gun: Maverick. Authorities have not released additional details about the circumstances surrounding the stabbing or the relationship between Handy and the suspect.

cards.headline: Questlove Discusses Earth, Wind & Fire Documentary and Future Projects
cards.teaser: The Oscar-winning filmmaker explains why he will probably never make a Prince documentary in a new interview.
cards.body:
Ahmir "Questlove" Thompson discussed his latest documentary project on Earth, Wind & Fire, arriving on HBO this weekend. The film, titled Earth, Wind Fire (to Be Celestial vs. Thats the Weight of the World), marks his fourth documentary following Summer of Soul, which won both an Oscar and a Grammy, along with Sly Lives and Ladies and Gentlemen, 50 Years of Saturday Night Live Music.

In the interview, Questlove addressed the possibility of making a documentary about Prince, stating he will probably never tackle that project. The drummer and leader of the Roots has established himself as a documentary filmmaker focused on music history and cultural figures. His work has received critical acclaim for exploring the contributions of Black artists to American music.

cards.headline: Madonna Announces YouTube Release of Confessions II Film
cards.teaser: The pop star will release the concert film on YouTube next week following its world premiere at the Tribeca Film Festival.
cards.body:
Madonna announced that Confessions II The Film will be released on YouTube on June 8 at 11 a.m. ET. The film, directed by David Toro and Solomon Chase, is set to have its world premiere at the Beacon Theatre in New York City as part of the Tribeca Film Festival.

The announcement marks a direct-to-digital release strategy for the concert film. The directors, known professionally as Torso, captured Madonna's performance for the project. The YouTube release will make the film available to a global audience immediately following its festival debut.

cards.headline: Paramount Unveils Changes to CBS Late Night and 60 Minutes at Upfront Presentation
cards.teaser: Advertising and media buying executives gathered to see what the newly restructured company would offer under CEO David Ellison.
cards.body:
I appreciate you sharing this material, but I need to flag an issue: the source articles provided are opinion pieces and news reports about consequences of changes to 60 Minutes (staff departures, internal conflict), not about Paramount's actual upfront presentation or what changes were announced there.

The Guardian articles discuss fallout from the restructuring—including Scott Pelley's firing and remaining correspondents' decisions to stay—but they don't describe what Paramount actually presented to advertisers at the upfront event regarding programming changes.

Since the additional sources don't contain confirmed details about the upfront presentation itself, I'm returning your original card text unchanged. To rewrite it properly, I would need sources that describe the actual programming changes Paramount presented to advertisers.

cards.headline: Lisa Kudrow and Michael Patrick King Discuss The Comeback's Return to HBO
cards.teaser: The creators reflect on the series ending, Valerie Cherish's evolution, and the unintentionally meta nature of the show's title.
cards.body:
Lisa Kudrow and Michael Patrick King discussed the return of their HBO comedy The Comeback, noting the series has made a comeback every ten years since its debut. The creators told Variety that the title has proven more meta than they initially intended. The show follows Valerie Cherish, a character whose evolution has been tracked across the series' sporadic returns.

In the interview, Kudrow and King addressed the series ending, the threat of AI in entertainment, and various aspects of the show's production. They also discussed why they believe ice cream as a dessert is, in their words, not acceptable. The conversation covered the creative decisions behind the character's development over the show's intermittent run on HBO.

cards.headline: Netflix Releases Mexico 86 Documentary Ahead of World Cup
cards.teaser: The Diego Luna-fronted film offers a behind-the-scenes look at a World Cup campaign as the tournament prepares to begin in North America.
cards.body:
Netflix released Mexico 86, a documentary featuring Diego Luna that examines a World Cup campaign. The film focuses on behind-the-scenes aspects rather than on-pitch action, offering viewers insight into the preparations and organization surrounding the tournament.

The release timing coincides with the FIFA World Cup beginning next week in the United States, Canada, and Mexico. This marks the first time three nations have simultaneously hosted the tournament, making Mexico the first country to host the World Cup three times.

hero.headline: House panel advances $1.15 trillion defense bill with accountability measures for Hegseth
hero.body:
The House Armed Services Committee advanced a $1.15 trillion defense policy bill early Friday, setting the stage for what would be the largest defense authorization in U.S. history. The legislation includes pay raises for service members, support for U.S. allies, and acquisition reforms.

The bill also includes provisions requiring increased accountability from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, reflecting bipartisan frustration with his leadership. The accountability measures come as some lawmakers from both parties have expressed concerns about oversight and transparency at the Pentagon under Hegseth's tenure.

The National Defense Authorization Act represents a significant increase in military spending and sets policy priorities for the Department of Defense. In addition to personnel pay increases, the legislation supports ongoing commitments to U.S. allies and implements reforms aimed at streamlining how the Pentagon acquires equipment and weapons systems.

The committee's vote sends the bill to the full House for consideration. The NDAA has historically enjoyed strong bipartisan support and is one of the few major pieces of legislation that Congress passes annually. The inclusion of provisions targeting Hegseth suggests lawmakers are using the must-pass bill as leverage to demand greater oversight of Pentagon operations.

The $1.15 trillion price tag reflects the scale of U.S. defense commitments worldwide and represents a continuation of increased military spending in recent years. The legislation will need to be reconciled with a Senate version before it can reach President Trump's desk for signature.

cards.headline: Senate Democrats call for halt to Trump-image gold coins
cards.teaser: Two senators raised concerns that some gold used by the U.S. Mint could be traced to foreign cartels.
cards.body:
Senators Elizabeth Warren and Ron Wyden called on the Trump administration Thursday to stop producing a 24-karat gold coin bearing President Trump's image. The coin is intended to commemorate America's 250th birthday.

The Democratic senators expressed concerns that some of the gold used by the U.S. Mint in the coin's production could be traced to foreign cartels. The lawmakers are seeking to halt the commemorative coin program until questions about the gold's sourcing can be addressed.

cards.headline: Trump faces potential lame duck status as agenda meets resistance
cards.teaser: The president needs congressional support to pass his agenda, but some controversial moves may be straining his relationship with Republicans.
cards.body:
President Trump is encountering obstacles in advancing his legislative priorities as some of his more controversial decisions appear to be affecting his relationship with Republicans on Capitol Hill. The president requires congressional cooperation to implement much of his policy agenda.

The dynamic raises questions about whether Trump could become an early lame duck, unable to move major legislation despite his party's presence in Congress. Some Republican lawmakers have begun expressing reservations about certain presidential actions, creating potential roadblocks for the administration's policy goals.

cards.headline: Former Border Patrol commander spoke at far-right international conference
cards.teaser: Greg Bovino appeared at a gathering alongside white supremacists and neo-Nazis.
cards.body:
Former Border Patrol commander Greg Bovino recently spoke at an international far-right gathering, according to reports. The event included appearances by white supremacists and neo-Nazis.

Bovino's participation in the conference raises questions about his associations and views. The former Border Patrol official held a senior command position within the agency before his recent appearance at the gathering.

cards.headline: Deb Haaland wins New Mexico Democratic primary for governor
cards.teaser: The former Biden administration official could become the first female Native American governor if elected.
cards.body:
Deb Haaland won the Democratic primary for governor of New Mexico on Friday. Haaland previously served in the Biden administration before launching her gubernatorial campaign.

If Haaland wins the general election, she would make history as the first female Native American governor in the United States. The primary victory positions her as the Democratic nominee heading into the November election.

cards.headline: California governor primary results show Hilton and Becerra leading
cards.teaser: Democrats Katie Porter, Tom Steyer, and Xavier Becerra face Republicans Chad Bianco and Steve Hilton in the race to replace Gavin Newsom.
cards.body:
Steve Hilton, a British-born conservative pundit, narrowly leads California's governor primary with an estimated 60% of ballots counted by Friday morning. Xavier Becerra, former US health and human services secretary under President Biden, follows closely behind, while billionaire Tom Steyer trails the pair.

Under California's primary system, the top two vote-getters advance to the general election in November regardless of party affiliation. Vote-counting is expected to continue for several days as election officials process remaining ballots.

cards.headline: Graham Platner denies relationship allegations, says campaign gaining momentum
cards.teaser: The Maine Senate candidate denied a New York Times report about being physically rough with former girlfriends.
cards.body:
Maine Senate candidate Graham Platner is rejecting accusations that he was physically rough with former girlfriends, according to reporting by The New York Times. He characterized the allegations as part of a pattern of controversies surrounding his candidacy.

Rather than viewing these incidents negatively, Platner interprets them as signs his campaign is gaining momentum. He has made clear he intends to remain in the Maine Senate race.
